**Answer: Yes.**

**Proof.**

Recall that the conjugate closure $\langle A^K\rangle$ is the normal closure of $A$ in $K$: the smallest normal subgroup of $K$ containing $A$, equivalently the subgroup generated by all conjugates $kak^{-1}$ with $k\in K$, $a\in A$. In particular $\langle A^K\rangle \unlhd K$.

Since $N\unlhd K$ and $\langle A^K\rangle\unlhd K$, the quotient map $q:K\to K/N$ sends $\langle A^K\rangle$ to a normal subgroup of $K/N$:
$$q(\langle A^K\rangle)\unlhd K/N.$$
Moreover $q(A)\subseteq q(\langle A^K\rangle)$, since $A\subseteq\langle A^K\rangle$.

The subgroup $\langle(q(A))^{K/N}\rangle$ is, by definition, the smallest normal subgroup of $K/N$ containing $q(A)$. Since $q(\langle A^K\rangle)$ is a normal subgroup of $K/N$ containing $q(A)$, minimality gives
$$\langle(q(A))^{K/N}\rangle \subseteq q(\langle A^K\rangle).$$

Now $q|_{\langle A^K\rangle}:\langle A^K\rangle\to K/N$ is a group homomorphism, and its image is exactly $q(\langle A^K\rangle)$. A homomorphic image of an Abelian group is Abelian, so by the hypothesis that $\langle A^K\rangle$ is Abelian,
$$q(\langle A^K\rangle)\text{ is Abelian}.$$

Finally, $\langle(q(A))^{K/N}\rangle$ is a subgroup of the Abelian group $q(\langle A^K\rangle)$, and every subgroup of an Abelian group is Abelian. Therefore
$$\langle(q(A))^{K/N}\rangle\text{ is Abelian}.\qquad\blacksquare$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
